newsitem.title: UK: NatWest admits weak controls in option loss.
newsitem.headline: NatWest admits weak controls in option loss.

text.p: National Westminster Bank on Thursday admitted weakness in its control procedures had contributed to a 90 million pounds ($150 million) loss in its interest rate options trading.
It said the losses were deliberately hidden over two years by the creation of false profits and unauthorised transfers between different books.

"The losses...went undiscovered because of deliberate concealment and weaknesses in the operations and internal controls in this area," the bank said in a statement. "The independent price checking regime...did not have sufficiently robust procedures for procuring external quotations and checking the pricing of options."
NatWest said improvements to the system, which were already being made, had helped detect the losses in February.
It also said that recommendations for improvements to the controls and risk management systems made by the investigation team are already being implemented.

The loss will show up as 77 million pounds in the books of the bank's investment banking unit NatWest Markets, after taking into account provisions and the clawing back of eight million pounds in bonuses.
But the bank has already admitted that the affair has led to poor trading in the first half and last week issued a profits warning affecting the whole group.
It also announced that NatWest Markets chief executive Martin Owen has left the firm and that group chief executive Derek Wanless will run the investment bank for the time being.

NatWest said on Thursday that the losses, contrary to City rumours, were confined to interest rate options business. But, to add to its discomfort, Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) announced it was now actively considering whether to launch a criminal investigation.

Five senior staff at NatWest Markets have resigned after it was found that the losses went undiscovered due to deliberate concealment and control weakness and that trader Kyriacos Papouis, who left NatWest in December 1996, covered up losses and created false profits over two years.

The report into the losses, first discovered in February, by law firm Linklaters & Paines and accountants Coopers & Lybrand, found that the losses in mark and sterling interest rate options had been due to poor trading and adverse market conditions.

The losses were then covered up, by deliberate mis-pricing and over-valuing of options contracts but NatWest said there was no evidence of client loss and no personal gain "as a result of collusion with third parties".

But NatWest said the full report is not being published for legal and commercial reasons, although it had been sent to the Bank of England and City regulator the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA). The SFO had also been fully briefed, it said.

Those resigning from NatWest Markets include Neil Dodgson, who was global head of interest rate options, Jean-Francois Nguyen, global head of swaps and derivatives and Ian Gaskell, head of swaps and options trading.

Andrew Grout, manager of the London position-keeping team, has also resigned as a result of findings that he failed in his duty to alert senior management to unusual positions and transactions, NatWest said.
Philip Wise, head of debt capital markets from November 1995 to December 1996, has also accepted responsibility and resigned, but will be compensated for the term of his contract.

Gaskell will complete a three-month notice period and will receive no further compensation while Nguyen, Dodgson and Grout will receive no payment. The head of rate risk management, Christophe Lanson, is to leave the company but "is not considered to be responsible for the losses and false profits", NatWest said. ($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
